title: Separating words problem
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that any two distinct binary words of length \(n\ge1\) can be distinguished by a deterministic finite automaton with at most \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states? Distinguishing means accepting exactly one of the two words, with unrestricted behavior on all other words. The automaton may depend on the pair, and its complete one-pass transition model is defined below.
why: Determining the polynomial exponent would quantify the worst-case finite-state memory needed to distinguish two long binary words, while separating polynomial growth from finer logarithmic factors.
status_note: The checked 2026 preprints retain a general one-third-power upper-bound scale and do not give matching asymptotics or a universal logarithmic bound. Read on 13 September 2026; proofs were not independently verified and the literature search was bounded.

progress.text: The source poses a logarithmic upper-bound target and mentions a one-third-power bound as an intermediate scale.

sentences: Two distinct binary strings are given at the same length.
A separating deterministic finite automaton must accept exactly one of them.
The question asks whether a logarithmic number of states always suffices.
The automaton may depend on both strings and has no restriction on other inputs.
This is stronger than merely asking whether the polynomial growth exponent is zero.

definitions:
The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton.

Precisely, write
\[
s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}
\min\bigl\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\bigr\}.
\]
The maximum and minimum use the model above. A complete DFA recognizing one fixed length-\(n\) word has at most \(n+2\) states, so \(1\le s(n)\le n+2\).

The assertion \(s(n)=O(\log n)\) is expressed for all positive lengths using \(\log_2(n+1)\). One universal constant must cover every length and every pair of distinct words; no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing the separating automaton.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.

context_blocks.text: The selected binary target is the original logarithmic-state question. A universal logarithmic bound would imply polynomial growth exponent zero, whereas exponent zero alone also permits faster-than-polylogarithmic growth. The owner’s later binary-target instruction supersedes the earlier numerical-exponent version of this card.

The August 2026 primary abstract reports a general \(\widetilde O(n^{1/3})\) upper bound and studies a stronger result only when one word is random. The September preprint supplies another proof at the general one-third exponent, not a logarithmic universal bound.
